title: 06: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering Techniques
text:
2 Getting Started

2.1 The Analytical Question
In real world application likes geobusiness and geospatail related policy making, regions are defined by statistical similarity in the multivariate data. In the case study of Shan State Myanmar, we find and outline the clusters of areas that share similar characteristics, through multiple Information and Communication technology (ICT) measures, namely: Radio, Television, Land line phone, Mobile phone, Computer, and Internet at home.

title: 06: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering Techniques
text:
3 The Data







Dataset
Description
Format



myanmar_township_boundaries
GIS Myanmar Township Boundary Data represented as polygon features
ESRI shapefile


Shan-ICT.csv
2014 Myanmar Population and Housing Census at the township level
CSV



The data can be downloaded from Myanmar Information Management Unit (MIMU).

3.1 Installing and Loading R Packages
There are 14 packages used in this exercise.

Spatial data (sf, spdep, tmap)
Cluster analysis (ClustGeo, cluster, NbClust, factoextra)
Multivariate exploration (corrplot, heatmaply, psych, GGally)
Visualisation / general workflow (tidyverse, ggpubr)



Package
Description



sf
Handles importing, managing, and processing vector-based geospatial data


rgdal
Provides bindings to the GDAL/OGR library for reading/writing spatial data formats.


spdep
Tools for spatial dependence: building neighbour lists, spatial weights, and spatial autocorrelation analysis.


tidyverse
A collection of R packages for data wrangling and visualisation, including readr, dplyr, and ggplot2.


tmap
Creates cartographic quality static and interactive thematic (choropleth) maps.


corrplot
Provides graphical displays of correlation matrices for multivariate data exploration.


ggpubr
Simplifies publication-ready plots based on ggplot2 with statistical annotations.


heatmaply
Generates interactive heatmaps for exploring multivariate data relationships.


cluster
Functions for cluster analysis, including hierarchical, partitioning, and silhouette methods.


ClustGeo
Performs spatially constrained clustering by balancing attribute similarity with geographical contiguity.


NbClust
Determines the optimal number of clusters using multiple indices and methods.


facoextra
Visualisation tools for clustering and multivariate analyses (e.g., PCA, CA, HCPC).


GGally
Extension of ggplot2 with functions for pair plots, network plots, and correlation plots.


psych
Procedures for psychometric and multivariate analysis, including factor analysis.



The code chunk below loads the packages into R environment.

pacman::p_load(spdep, tmap, sf, ClustGeo, 
               ggpubr, cluster, factoextra, NbClust,
               heatmaply, corrplot, psych, tidyverse, GGally, knitr)

title: 06: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering Techniques
text:
5 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

5.1 EDA Using Statistical Graphics
To examine the variables such as the number of households with radio, we can use graphical methods that highlight different aspects of the data distribution:
Histogram

Shows the overall shape of the distribution.
Helps identify whether the data is left-skewed, right-skewed, or approximately normal.
Useful for understanding the frequency of values and detecting clustering or gaps in the data.


ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
       aes(x=`RADIO`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")







Boxplot:

Summarises the distribution using the five-number summary (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum).
Makes it easy to detect outliers and understand the spread and central tendency of the data.
Allows quick comparison across multiple variables or groups (e.g., by township).


ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
       aes(x= RADIO )) +
  geom_boxplot(color="black", 
               fill="light blue")







Let’s also visualise the distribution of the newly derived variables (i.e. Radio penetration rate).

ggplot(data = ict_derived,
       aes(x = RADIO_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")








ggplot(data = ict_derived,
       aes(x = RADIO_PR)) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "black", fill = "light blue")













Note




What can you observed from the distributions reveal in the histogram and boxplot?

The penetration rate data are more normally distributed and show fewer outliers than the raw ownership counts, since the effect of township size has been normalised.


In the figure below, multiple histograms are plotted to reveal the distribution of the selected variables in the ict_derived data.frame.
In tmap, tmap_arrange() (or tmarange) is used to arrange multiple map plots side by side or in a grid layout.
In ggplot2, the equivalent is ggarrange() from the ggpubr package.

View coderadio <- ggplot(data= ict_derived,
                aes(x = RADIO_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue")

tv <- ggplot(data = ict_derived, aes(x= TV_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue")

llphone <- ggplot(data = ict_derived, aes(x = LLPHONE_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black",fill = "light blue")

mphone <- ggplot(data = ict_derived, aes(x = MPHONE_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue")

computer <- ggplot(data = ict_derived, aes(x = COMPUTER_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill ="light blue") 

internet <- ggplot(data = ict_derived, aes(x = INTERNET_PR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue")

ggarrange(radio, tv, llphone, mphone, computer, internet, 
          ncol = 3,
          nrow = 2)








5.2 EDA Using Choropleth Map

5.2.1 Joining Geospatial Data with Aspatial Data
Previously we use the ggplot2 to visualise the distribution and outliers of the ICT variables in the tibble data.frame ict_derived. To incorporate the statistical data with corresponding township locations, we now use left_join() function from the dplyr package to combine the two data sets ( shan_sf as an sf data.frame and ict_derived) based on the primary key ‘TS_PCODE’. We then plot a choropleth map of the selected variable distribution using the qtm() function from the tmap package. The code chunk below performs the above-mentioned first step.

shan_sf <- left_join(shan_sf, ict_derived, by = c("TS_PCODE" = "TS_PCODE"))
write_rds(shan_sf, "data/rds/shan_sf.rds") #save for further analysis


shan_sf  <- read_rds("data/rds/shan_sf.rds")


5.2.2 Preparing a Choropleth Map
The code chunk below uses the qtm() function from the tmap package to create a choropleth map that visualises the spatial distribution of radio penetration rates across Shan State townships.

qtm(shan_sf, "RADIO_PR")







Next let’s visualise why it is important to transform absolute values to relative measures before performing spatial analysis. Otherwise the results could be biased. The difference becomes clear when we comparing the distribution of the total number households across townships (TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map) with the distribution of households owning Radio (Radio.map).
The code chunk plot two choropleth maps and arrange them side by side.

TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) + 
  tm_fill("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", # colour or numeric or categorical variable in `shp` 
          n = 5,
          style = "jenks",  # preferred number of classes for numeric 'col' 
          title = "Total households", textNA = NA) +
   tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "top")) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) 

RADIO.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) + 
  tm_fill( "RADIO",
          n = 5,
          style = "jenks",
          title = "Number Radio ",textNA = NA) + 
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "top")) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) 

tmap_arrange(TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map, RADIO.map, 
             asp=1, ncol=2)  #Aspect ratio of each map








any(is.na(shan_sf))

[1] FALSE



tm_shape(shan_sf) +
    tm_polygons(c("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", "RADIO_PR"),
                style="jenks", textNA = NA) +
    tm_facets(sync = TRUE, ncol = 2) +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_layout(outer.margins=0, asp=0)













Note




Can you identify the differences?

Although the penetration rate map partly mirrors the distribution of total households, radio ownership does not scale one-to-one with township population. Other factors (e.g., income, market access etc) influence adoption, so using relative measures such as penetration rate reduces size bias and provides a more accurate basis for clustering and spatial comparisons than raw counts.








Tip




Jenks: Reveals natural clusters in skewed data by minimising within-class variance.

Tip: Great for one-off maps; for comparisons, compute once and use fixed breaks.

Equal interval: Splits the value range into equal-width bins. simple and consistent.

Tip: Best when data are fairly uniform or when you need fixed policy thresholds.

Quantile: Puts an equal number of features in each class, highlighting ranks/percentiles.

Tip: Ensures balanced colours; watch for tiny value differences flipping classes.

Pretty: Uses rounded, human-friendly breakpoints for clean legends.

Tip: Ideal for communication; double-check that the bins still reflect the data distribution.

title: 06: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering Techniques
text:
6 Correlation Analysis
Before running cluster analysis, we should check correlations between variables. If a pair is highly correlated (e.g., |r| >= 0.8), one of the pair should be dropped to avoid redundancy. The code chunk below uses corrplot.mixed() function from corrplot package to visualise the correlations.

cluster_vars.cor = cor(ict_derived[,12:17]) #corr matrix
corrplot.mixed(cluster_vars.cor,  # use mixed method to visualise the matrix
               lower = "ellipse", # visualisation methods for lower triangular 
               upper = "number", ## visualisation methods for upper triangular 
               tl.pos = "lt",  #text label position: lt means left and top, d diagonal, n means no.
               diag ="l", #glyph in diagonal: n/l/u means no/lower/upper 
               tl.col = "black")







We observe that INTERNET_PR is highly correlated with COMPUTER_PR (r = 0.87), so we will drop one of them from the cluster analysis to avoid redundancy.

title: 06: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering Techniques
text:
7 Hiearachy Cluster Anlaysis
The general workflow of hierarchy cluster analysis consists of:

Extracting clustering variables (screen for NAs & high correlations). st_set_geometry(NULL); select(); row.names()
Standardising the variables (min-max/ z-scores). normalize(); scale()
Computing a proximity (distance) matrix (often Euclidean). dist()
Running hierarchical clustering (choose linkage, e.g., ward.D2). hclust();agnes()
Determining the optimal number of clusters (dendrogram + silhouette/gap/NbClust). clusGap(FUN = hcut)
Interpreting the dendrogram & profile clusters (cluster means, maps, tables).rect.hclust()
Visualisation (dendrogram, heatmap, spatial choropleths). heatmaply(), cutree(), cbind(), qtm()


7.1 Extracting Clustering Variables
The code chunk below extracts the 5 clustering variables (excluding INTERNET_PR) from shan_sf sf object to a new data.frame.

cluster_vars <- shan_sf %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL) %>% # or st_drop_geometry() removes the geometry
select("TS.x", "RADIO_PR", "TV_PR", "LLPHONE_PR", "MPHONE_PR", "COMPUTER_PR") # INTERNET_PR  is omitted

7.3 Computing Proximity Matrix
In R, several packages provide functions to calculate distance matrices. Here, we will use the dist() function of base R to compute a proximity matrix.
The function does not calculate geographic distance (like latitude–longitude great-circle distance).
Instead, it calculates mathematical distances in feature space, based on the values of the clustering variables (columns).






Note



dist(x, method = “euclidean”, diag = FALSE, upper = FALSE, p = 2)

x is a numeric matrix, data frame or dist object.
p is the power of the Minkowski distance.
6 methods include euclidean, maximum, manhattan, canberra, binary, and minkowski, with euclidean being the default.



The code chunk demonstrates how to generate a proximity matrix using the euclidean method.

proxmat <- dist(shan_ict,method="euclidean")


summary(proxmat)

7.4 Computing Hierachical Clustering
In R, several packages provide functions for hierarchical clustering. We use the hclust() function from base R to build clusters.
Thefunction applies an agglomerative approach (bottom up).






Note



hclust(d, method = “complete”, members = NULL)

d is a dist object
method supports eight clustering methods: ward.D, ward.D2, single, complete, average (UPGMA), mcquitty (WPGMA), median (WPGMC), and centroid (UPGMC).



The code chunk below computes hierarchical clustering using the ward.D method. The results are stored in an object of class hclust, which contains the tree structure (dendrogram) generated by the clustering process.

hclust_ward <- hclust(proxmat, method = "ward.D")
hclust_ward$labels[1]

[1] "Mongmit"

hclust_ward$height[1]

[1] 38.52842


The code chunk creates the tree by using plot() of R Graphics.

plot(hclust_ward, cex = 0.9) #shrink by 10%








7.5 Selecting the Optimal Clustering Algorithm
One challenge in hierarchical clustering is determining the stronger cluster structure. Unlike hclust(), the agnes() function from the cluster package directly returns the agglomerative coefficient (AC). When AC closer to 1, it indicates a stronger clustering structure.






Note



agnes(x, diss = inherits(x, “dist”), metric = “euclidean”, stand = FALSE, method = “average”, par.method, keep.diss = n < 100, keep.data = !diss, trace.lev = 0) agnes: short for Agglomerative Nesting.


Below, we compute the agglomerative coefficient for several linkage methods and compare them.

m <- c( "average", "single", "complete", "ward")        # creates a vector of methods
names(m) <- c( "average", "single", "complete", "ward") # gives each element a name

ac <- function(x) {
  agnes(shan_ict, method = x)$ac  #$ac extracts ac
}

map_dbl(m, ac) # applies the function ac() to each element of m.

  average    single  complete      ward 
0.8131144 0.6628705 0.8950702 0.9427730 



7.6 Determining Optimal Clusters
Another technical challenge is deciding on the optimal number of clusters to retain. Choosing too few clusters may oversimplify the data, while too many clusters may lead to overfitting and poor interpretability.
Three commonly used methods to determine the appropriate number of clusters are:
Elbow Method

Plots the total within-cluster sum of squares (WSS) against the number of clusters.
The “elbow” point, where the rate of decrease sharply slows, indicates a suitable number of clusters.

Average Silhouette Method

Computes the silhouette coefficient, which measures how similar an observation is to its own cluster compared to other clusters.
The number of clusters with the highest average silhouette value is considered optimal.

Gap Statistic Method

Compares the total within-cluster variation for k different numbers of clusters with the expected values under a null reference distribution.
The optimal number of clusters is the one that maximises the gap statistic.


7.6.1 Gap Statistic Method
The code chunk below uses clusGap() of cluster(https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/cluster/index.html) package to compute the gap statistics. The hcut() function used is from factoextra package.

set.seed(12345)
gap_stat <- clusGap(shan_ict, 
                    FUN = hcut, #hcut or kmeans
                    nstart = 25, #random starts for kmeans
                    K.max = 10, 
                    B = 50)  #bootstrap
# Print the result
print(gap_stat, method = "firstmax") # common ones: first(local)max, globalmax, tibs2001SEmax(first peak)

7.7 Interpreting the Dendrograms
In the dendrogram, each leaf represents an observation. Moving upward, similar observations are joined into branches, which then merge at higher levels. The vertical axis shows the fusion height, reflecting dissimilarity: lower values indicate greater similarity, while higher values mean less similarity. Similarity can only be inferred from the height at which branches first merge, not from their horizontal positions.

plot(hclust_ward, cex = 0.9) #shrink by 10%







We use rect.hclust() of R stats to draw the border boxes. border = 2:5 means: to use red, green, blue, and cyan as the rectangle borders.

plot(hclust_ward, cex = 0.9)
rect.hclust(hclust_ward, 
            k = 6, 
            border = 2:5)








7.8 Visually-driven Hierarchical Clustering Analysis

7.8.2 Plotting Interactive Cluster Heatmap using heatmaply()
The code chunk below uses heatmaply() heatmaply package to create interactive cluster heatmap.

          Colv=NA,
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "ward.D",
          seriate = "OLO",
          colors = Blues,
          k_row = 6,
          margins = c(NA,200,60,NA),
          fontsize_row = 4,
          fontsize_col = 5,
          main="Geographic Segmentation of Shan State by ICT indicators",
          xlab = "ICT Indicators",
          ylab = "Townships of Shan State"
          )

To visualise the clustering results, this list must be appended to the shan_sf simple feature object. The process can be carried out in three steps:

Convert the groups list into a matrix.
Use cbind() to attach this matrix to shan_sf, producing a new simple feature object called shan_sf_cluster.
Apply the rename() function from the dplyr package to change the column name from as.matrix.groups to CLUSTER.

Subsequently, the qtm() function from the tmap package is used to generate a choropleth map that displays the cluster results. The map shows that the clusters are highly fragmented, which highlights a key limitation of non-spatial clustering methods such as hierarchical cluster analysis.

shan_sf_cluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) %>%
  rename(`CLUSTER`=`as.matrix.groups.`)

title: 06: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering Techniques
text:
8 Spatially Constrained Clustering: SKATER approach
Next we use skater(https://r-spatial.github.io/spdep/reference/skater.html) from spdep to find spatially constrained cluster.
The skater() stands for Spatial ’K’luster Analysis by Tree Edge Removal.

8.1 Converting into SpatialPolygonsDataFrame
The code chunk below uses [as_Spatial()'](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/reference/coerce-methods.html) to coerceshan_sfassfinto Spatial*Polygons*DataFrame which can be processed byskater()`function later.

shan_sp <- as_Spatial(shan_sf)

title: 06: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering Techniques
text:
9 Spatially Constrained Clustering: ClustGeo Method
In this section, we perform non-spatially constrained hierarchical cluster analysis and spatially constrained cluster analysis with ClustGeo package.

9.1 A short note about ClustGeo package
ClustGeo is an R package for spatially constrained clustering.
It implements a Ward-like (variance-minimising) hierarchical method, hclustgeo(), that blends two dissimilarities:

D0: a dist object represents dissimilarity in the attribute space (can be non-Euclidean; observations may be weighted).
D1: a dist object represents dissimilarity in the spatial/constraint space.

A mixing parameter alpha (0,1) controls the trade-off via a convex combination of homogeneity criteria:
criterion= (1-a) * crit(D0) + a * crit*(D1)
The goal is to choose alpha to increase spatial contiguity without unduly harming cluster quality on the variables of interest. The function choicealpha() estimates a suitable alpha by comparing solutions across alpha values.






Note



hclustgeo(D0, D1 = NULL, alpha = 0, scale = TRUE, wt = NULL)

hclustgeo(D0) = non-spatial (standard Ward).
hclustgeo(D0, D1, alpha) = spatially constrained clustering.
Scale is used when both D0 and D1 are included, and scaled by i.e. divided by their max.




9.2 Ward-like hierarchical clustering: ClustGeo
hclustgeo() extends the base R function hclust(). Under the hood, it constructs a dendrogram object with the same structure as stats::hclust.
The code chunk below use hclustgeo() to perform hierarchical clustering.

nongeo_cluster <- hclustgeo(proxmat)
nongeo_cluster


Call:
stats::hclust(d = delta, method = "ward.D", members = wt)

Cluster method   : ward.D 
Distance         : euclidean 
Number of objects: 55 

plot(nongeo_cluster, cex = 0.5)
rect.hclust(nongeo_cluster, k = 6, border = 2:5) 






#`border = 2:5` means: to use **red, green, blue, and cyan** as the rectangle borders.


9.3 Mapping the clusters formed
The code chunk below plots the non-spatial constrained hierachical clustering.

groups <- as.factor(cutree(nongeo_cluster, k = 6))


shan_sf_ngeo_cluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) %>%
  rename(`CLUSTER` = `as.matrix.groups.`)


qtm(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, "CLUSTER")








hclust.map <- qtm(shan_sf_cluster, "CLUSTER") + 
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right","top")) +
  tm_title("Hierarchical Clustering (hclust)")

ngeohclust.map <- qtm(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, "CLUSTER") + 
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right","top")) +
  tm_title("Non-Spatially Constrained Hierarchical Clustering (hclustgeo)")

             asp = NA, ncol = 2)

text:
10 Visual Interpretation of Clusters

10.1 Visualising Individual Clustering Variable
The code chunk below visualises the distribution of a clustering variable (i.e. RADIO_PR) by cluster.

ggplot(data = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster,
       aes(x = CLUSTER, y = RADIO_PR)) +
  geom_boxplot()







The boxplot shows Cluster 3 has the highest Radio Ownership per thousand household on average and followed by Cluster 2, 1, 4, 5 and 6.

plot_boxplots <- function(var) {
  ggplot(data = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, aes(x = CLUSTER, y = .data[[var]])) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    labs( y = var)
  }
vars <- names(shan_ict)
for (v in vars) {print(plot_boxplots(v))}
































10.2 Multivariate Visualisation
The code chunk creates parallel coordinate plots to reveal clustering variables by cluster using ggparcoord() of GGally package.

ggparcoord(data = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster,
           columns = c(17:21),
           scale = "globalminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Multiple Paralle Coordinates Plots of ICT Variables by Cluster") +
  facet_grid(~ CLUSTER) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30))







The parallel coordinate plot shows that households in Cluster 4 townships tend to own the highest numbers of TVs and mobile phones, whereas households in Cluster 5 townships record the lowest ownership across all five ICT assets.
Below is a summary of the scale options in ggparcoord():


std: standardise by mean and standard deviation.

robust: standardise by median and median absolute deviation.

uniminmax: rescale each variable to [0, 1] range.

globalminmax: no scaling; all variables share the same global min–max.

center: uniminmax scaling, then centre at a chosen summary value.

centerObs: uniminmax scaling, then centre at a chosen observation.

There is no universally best method.
Finally, the code chunk below calculates summary statistics such as mean, median, sd, etc.

shan_sf_ngeo_cluster %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL) %>% #also when we extract clustering variable
  group_by(CLUSTER) %>%
  summarise(mean_RADIO_PR = mean(RADIO_PR),
            mean_TVO_PR = mean(TV_PR),
            mean_LLPHONE_PR = mean(LLPHONE_PR),
            mean_MPHONE_PR = mean(MPHONE_PR),
            mean_COMPUTER_PR = mean(COMPUTER_PR))

section: 8 Hedonic Pricing Modelling Using Functions from Base R
text:
8 Hedonic Pricing Modelling Using Functions from Base R
Next we build the hedonic pricing models for condominium reale units using lm() of base R.






Note




syntax:

lm(formula, data, subset, weights, na.action, method = “qr”, model = TRUE, x = FALSE, y = FALSE, qr = TRUE, singular.ok = TRUE, contrasts = NULL, offset, …)



8.1 Simple Linear Regression Method
First, the code chunk below build a simple linear regression model that predicts SELLING_PRICE based on AREA_SQM.The tilde (~) is read as “is modelled by” or “as a function of.”

condo.slr <-lm(formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM, data = condo_resale.sf)

The code chunk blow prints the model call from R’s lm() linear model function and model’s coefficients.

condo.slr


Call:
lm(formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM, data = condo_resale.sf)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)     AREA_SQM  
    -258121        14719  


The code chunk below returns the summary report of the simple regression model.

Residuals rules:



Residuals Statistic
Interpretation



Median approx 0
unbiased model overall


Negative median
Overestimate on average


Positive median
Underestimate on average



Since the median is negative -87K, the model slightly overestimates the selling prices.

Coefficients:

The linear relationship can be described as:
SELLING_PRICE = -258121.1 + 14719.0 x AREA_SQM
That means every one sqm increases in area will result in $14,719 increases in selling price on average. Since selling price is not below zero in real life, the intercept has no practical meaning. Since p-values of coefficients are much smaller than 0.001,we reject the null hypothesis that both coefficient are statistically significant.

Model fit Statistics

Residual standard error of 942,700 means that the predictions are about $942,700 away from the actual prices on average. The R-squared 0.4518 means the simple linear model can explain 45% of variance in resale prices. The p-value of F-statistics (< 0.001) confirms that the simple model is statistically significant.

The corrplot package is used because the pairs() from base R output can be cramped and difficult to interpret when there are many variables. 8.6 Regression Diagnostics
Regression model’s assumptions are:

Linearity: Predictors have linear relation to target
Independence: Errors are independent

Normality: Errors are normally distributed, QQ plot
No Multicollinearity: Predictors not highly correlated

In this section, we use olsrr package to perform the OLS regression diagnostics.

If the model’s residuals (the differences between observed and predicted values) are normally distributed, the normality assumption holds. This is crucial for accurate hypothesis testing and confidence intervals.

The hedonic model uses geographically referenced data, thus it is essential to check for spatial autocorrelation. Traditional OLS regression assumes independent observations, but spatial data often violates this assumption. Spatial autocorrelation occurs when nearby locations exhibit similar (positive) or dissimilar (negative) values, consistent with Tobler’s First Law of Geography. Ignoring it can lead to biased coefficients, incorrect p-values, and model misspecification. Therefore, testing the model’s residuals with Moran’s I is necessary—significant spatial autocorrelation indicates that the model fails to capture important spatial effects.

ols_test_correlation(condo.mlr1)

[1] 0.8254074


The OLS autocorrelation value of 0.825 suggests strong positive autocorrelation that the residuals are not independent. This violates the OLS assumption of error independence and should be further tested using Moran’s I for spatial dependence. Significant spatial autocorrelation in the residuals means the model is not capturing the full spatial story, some spatial dependence is left unexplained.
We first save the residuals as a data frame.

mlr.output <- as.data.frame(condo.mlr1$residuals)

Next,we join the residuals with condo_resale.sf object.

condo_resale.sf <- cbind(condo_resale.sf, mlr.output) %>%
  rename(`MLR_RES`= `condo.mlr1.residuals`)

Next, we plot the distribution of residuals using functions from tmap package on an interactive map.

tmap_mode("view")


tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill_alpha =0.4) +
  tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +
  tm_dots( fill = "MLR_RES",
           size = 0.7,
           col = "black",
           fill.scale = tm_scale(
             n= 10,
             value = rev(brewer.pal(11, "RdBu")),
             style = "quantile",
             midpoint = NA),
           fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residuals")) +
  
  tm_title("LM Residuals (Quantile Classification)") +
  tm_layout(legdend.outside = TRUE) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(11,14))







tmap_mode("plot")

Each dot represents a condo resale residual (actual - predicted):

Green dots (positive): model underpredicted (actual > predicted).
Purple dots (negative): model overpredicted (actual < predicted).

If residuals were spatially random, green and purple dots would be evenly scattered across Singapore.But it is not the case here. Further, the coexistence of overestimates and underestimates within the same region indicates that the OLS model cannot fully capture local variations in housing market dynamics.
Next we can confirm with Moran’s I test on residuals.
First, we compute distance-based weight matrix using st_dist_band() function of sfdep.

condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf %>%
  mutate(nb = st_dist_band(st_geometry(geometry), upper = 1500),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)

Then, we use global_moran_perm() of sfdep package conduct Moran’s I test for residual spatial autocorrelation with Monte Carlo Simulations (500 times).

set.seed(1234)
global_moran_perm(condo_resale.sf$MLR_RES,
                  nb = condo_resale.sf$nb,
                  wt = condo_resale.sf$wt,
                  alternative = "two.sided",
                  nsim = 499)


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  x 
weights: listw  
number of simulations + 1: 500 

statistic = 0.14389, observed rank = 500, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided


The Global Moran’s I value of 0.1439 (p < 0.05) indicates a statistically significant positive spatial autocorrelation, suggesting a mild clustering pattern across the study area.

title: 07: Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise Property with GWR Method
section: 9 Building Hedonic Pricing Models Using GWmodel Package
text:
9 Building Hedonic Pricing Models Using GWmodel Package
In this section, we build hedonic pricing models using both the fixed and adaptive bandwidth schemes.

9.1 Computing Fixed Bandwidth
The bw.gwr() function from the GWModel package determines the optimal fixed bandwidth (**adaptive** = FALSE) and uses a stopping rule based on either the cross-validation (CV) or AICc (AIC) approach, as specified by the approach argument. Here, we use the CV approach since it tends to produce a smaller bandwidth, which is more suitable for capturing local spatial variation.

bw.fixed <- bw.gwr(

    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL   + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP   + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + 
    FREEHOLD, 
  data=condo_resale.sf, 
  bw=bw.fixed, 
  kernel = 'gaussian', 
  longlat = FALSE)

9.3 Building Adaptive Bandwidth GWR Model
Next we calibrate the GWR-based hedonic pricing model by using adaptive bandwidth approach.

9.3.1 Computing the Adaptive Bandwidth
The code chunk below calculates the adaptive bandwidth by setting the adaptive argument to TRUE, allowing the bandwidth to vary according to the density of data points across the regions.

bw.adaptive <- bw.gwr(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE  + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE    +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + 
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL   + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP   + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + 
    FREEHOLD, 
  data=condo_resale.sf, 
  approach = "CV",
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)

9.5 Visualising GWR Output
The GWR output includes diagnostic and model evaluation fields stored in the sf DataFrame under the SDF output list. These contain the observed and predicted y values, residuals, condition numbers, local R2, explanatory variable coefficients, standard errors, and corresponding t-values.

Condition Number:

Assesses local multicollinearity. Values above 30 indicate unstable or unreliable local estimates.

Local R2: Indicates how well the local model fits observed data (0–1 range). Mapping these values highlights areas where the model performs well or poorly, revealing potential missing variables or spatial non-stationarity.
Predicted Values: The fitted y values estimated by the GWR.
Residuals: Differences between observed and predicted y; standardised residuals (mean = 0, SD = 1) can be mapped with a cold–hot colour scheme to visualise model performance.
Coefficient Standard Errors: Measure the reliability of coefficient estimates. Small standard errors relative to coefficient magnitudes indicate stable estimates, while large errors suggest local collinearity issues.

By jointly examining the Local R2 and residuals maps, we can identify areas where the model performs well (high Local R2, small residuals) and areas where it performs poorly (low Local R2, large residuals).

9.7 Visualising Local R2
The code chunks below is used to create an interactive point symbol map.

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(mpsz_svy21)+
  tm_polygons(fill_alpha = 0.1) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf.adaptive) +  
  tm_dots(col = "Local_R2",
          border.col = "gray60",
          border.lwd = 1) +
  tm_view(set.zoom.limits = c(11,14))





tmap_mode("plot")


9.8 Visualising Coefficient Estimates
The code chunks below is used to create an interactive point symbol map for AREA_SQM.

tmap_mode("view")
AREA_SQM_SE <- tm_shape(mpsz_svy21)+
  tm_polygons(alpha = 0.1) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf.adaptive) +  
  tm_dots(col = "AREA_SQM_SE",      #standard error of local coefficient, reliability of local estimate
          border.col = "gray60",
          border.lwd = 1) +
  tm_view(set.zoom.limits = c(11,14))

AREA_SQM_TV <- tm_shape(mpsz_svy21)+
  tm_polygons(alpha = 0.1) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf.adaptive) +  
  tm_dots(col = "AREA_SQM_TV",   # local t-value, statistical significance of local effect
          border.col = "gray60",
          border.lwd = 1) +
  tm_view(set.zoom.limits = c(11,14))

tmap_arrange(AREA_SQM_SE, AREA_SQM_TV, 
             asp=1, ncol=2,
             sync = TRUE)













tmap_mode("plot")

The spatial distribution of AREA_SQM coefficients indicates that floor area is a reliable and significant predictor of condominium prices in the central and south-eastern regions, where standard errors are lower and t-values are moderate to high. In contrast, the northern and western regions exhibit higher standard errors and lower t-values. The floor area has a less stable and weaker influence on price variation in these areas.
The code chunks below is used to create an interactive point symbol map for MRT.

PROX_MRT_SE <- tm_shape(mpsz_svy21)+
  tm_polygons(alpha = 0.1) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf.adaptive) +  
  tm_dots(col = "PROX_MRT_SE",      #standard error of local coefficient, reliability of local estimate
          border.col = "gray60",
          border.lwd = 1) +
  tm_view(set.zoom.limits = c(11,14))

PROX_MRT_TV <- tm_shape(mpsz_svy21)+
  tm_polygons(alpha = 0.1) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf.adaptive) +  
  tm_dots(col = "PROX_MRT_TV",   # local t-value, statistical significance of local effect
          border.col = "gray60",
          border.lwd = 1) +
  tm_view(set.zoom.limits = c(11,14))

tmap_arrange(PROX_MRT_SE, PROX_MRT_TV, 
             asp=1, ncol=2,
             sync = TRUE)







The PROX_MRT variable exhibits low standard errors overall, that means stable coefficient estimates across the study area. It shows a strong and statistically significant negative relationship with condominium resale prices in the central and southern subzones. That properties closer to MRT stations tend to have higher prices.
However, a few light-coloured subzones, such as Bukit Batok, Bukit Panjang, Bukit Timah, and several areas along the East Coast exhibit non-significant relationships.
|t| < 1.96 means statistically insignificant.

In sf package, there are two functions that can be used to combine multiple simple features into a single geometry: st_combine() and st_union().

st_combine() merges multiple geometries into one without resolving their internal boundaries. As a result, the combined geometry may not be valid.
st_union() is more versatile and intelligent. It merges and resolves their shared boundaries (removing overlaps and gaps).

3 Introducing spatstat Package
spatstat is a comprehensive R package for analysing two-dimensional spatial point patterns, including multitype and marked points, within any spatial region. A marked pattern refers to a point pattern where each point has an associated attribute (categorical or numeric), such as tree species or height. A multitype pattern is a special case of a marked pattern where the mark is categorical, such as restaurant or café.

text:
13 Edge correction methods of spatstat
In spatstat, edge correction methods adjust for boundary-related biases in spatial point pattern analysis, ensuring more accurate estimation of summary functions like the K, L, and pair correlation functions.
Common Edge Correction Methods in spatstat

“none”: No edge correction is applied. This approach assumes there is no boundary bias, which can result in underestimation of statistics for points near the edges of the study region.

-“isotropic”: Assumes the point pattern is isotropic (uniform in all directions). It compensates for missing neighbours outside the observation window by adjusting distances based on the proportion of the circle lying within the boundary.

“translate” (Translation Correction): Applies a translation correction, in which the observation window is translated so that each point is fully contained within it. The statistic is then averaged over all possible translations to correct for edge bias.
“Ripley” (Ripley’s Correction): A correction designed specifically for Ripley’s K-function and related summary functions. It adjusts the expected number of neighbours for edge points according to the shape and area of the observation window.
“border”: Also known as the reduced-sample correction, this method considers only those points whose neighbourhoods are entirely contained within the observation window. It is conservative but effectively minimises edge bias.

Since the L-function is commonly used in spatial point pattern analysis and is derived from Ripley’s K-function, the “Ripley” edge correction is generally appropriate choice among Edge Correction Methods.
